newsitem.title: USA: Fed's Meyer says Fed not restrictive in '96 - sources.
newsitem.headline: Fed's Meyer says Fed not restrictive in '96 - sources.

text.p: Federal Reserve Governor Laurence Meyer said on Thursday monetary policy in 1996 was not as restrictive as U.S. policymakers thought at the time, according to market sources.
Meyer made his remarks in a question-and-answer session at a Forecasters Club of New York luncheon, an event that was closed to the press.
"Meyer said, 'Policy was not as restrictive as we thought,'" a source who attended the event told Reuters.

The source said Meyer was referring to Fed policy in 1996 when the central bank lowered the benchmark federal funds rate to 5.25 percent on January 31, 1996, and left it at that level for the rest of the year.

The source quoted Meyer as saying that what convinced him to vote for the Fed's 25-basis-point hike in the funds rate on March 25 was "not so much one particular thing," but incoming early 1997 data that "created a collection of stories ... that suggested above-trend growth."
Meyer, like other Fed officials, also acknowledged that tight labor markets were a key concern for the Fed.

Meyer, who previously headed a forecasting firm known for its economic models, was asked to comment on monetary policy and the Phillips curve theory or the relation between tight labor markets and inflationary pressures.

Answering a question about where he believes the non-accelerating inflation rate of unemployment (NAIRU) is, Meyer said, according to the source, "data suggest to me the NAIRU is lower than I would have estimated it two years ago... at about 5.5 percent" (jobless rate).
Meyer, who said he earlier estimated NAIRU at around 6.0 percent, added that uncertainty about the rate remains.

Asked about whether the Fed believes the U.S. labor force can continue to grow at a higher-than-expected rate of about 2.0 percent, Meyer answered it's "a fundamental problem," according to the source.
The monetary policy implications of a higher-than-expected labor force growth rate would be that trend growth can run above 2.25- to 2.50 percent without generating inflation.

The source also said Meyer stated the Fed should not have to defend policy decisions such as the March 25 tightening. The first such move in more than two years, it followed three small easing steps taken between mid-1995 and early 1996.
Meyer stressed "there is too much emphasis on defending reversals" of policy, the source said.
Asked about the impact of the dollar on monetary policy, Meyer was quoted as saying "it's one of a host of variables."

In prepared remarks that were made available to the press, Meyer earlier on Thursday warned the U.S. "economy appears to be growing at an unsustainable above-trend rate" which "requires that real interest rates rise as long as growth is above-trend and utilization rates are rising."
Meyer's comments in the question-and-answer session were confirmed by another source.
